Article Title: A taste for good food and brutal knockouts: Carlos Prates on India's charm and his UFC title dream
Article Text:
​Carlos Prates

Carlos Prates in India

Life outside the Octagon

Carlos Prates

Six years in Thailand and the grind before the UFC

From Contender Series to a run of seven UFC wins

Makhachev setback and an interim title opportunity

islam makhachev

Michael Morales: The unbeaten challenge facing Prates

Michales Morales

Alex Pereira, legacy and what comes next

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Carlos Prates had a fair bit to tick off during his India visit. There was the food, the traditional attire, the local culture and, going by his social media updates, even some firecracker fun. The Brazilian UFC fighter is enjoying himself, making the most of a visit that was as much about experiencing India as it was about connecting with its sporting audience.“I’m really enjoying India. The food is amazing, the people are amazing. I like the culture, everything. India is one of the places I’ve always wanted to visit,” Prates told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive interaction on Saturday.Prates is in India as part of the UFC India Tour, aimed at bringing UFC fighters closer to fans. For the Brazilian, the visit was as much about meeting people and experiencing a new culture as it was about representing the UFC.“I like to travel, meet people, talk to people, try different food. I like to know different cultures,” he said.However, there was one popular Indian obsession he had not quite figured out. Asked about cricket, Prates admitted he knew little about the sport, despite being aware of its following in India."I know cricket is really famous here in India, but I don't know the rules," he said.The 33-year-old is known for his knockout power inside the Octagon, but there is a noticeably different side to him away from fight night. He enjoys a party, likes spending time with friends and family, and is generally comfortable striking up conversations with people.But, He draws a clear line between the two sides of his life. "No, bro. I'm always like this," he said when asked whether he switches personalities between fight night and everyday life. "Inside the Octagon, I need to be serious because it's my work, my health and my family's money. My daughter and my mother are there. But outside the Octagon, it's different. I like talking to everybody and having fun with everybody."That easy-going attitude has not come from an easy journey in the sport. Before becoming one of the UFC's most explosive welterweights, Prates had to go through the proper grind in MMA, including spending six years in Thailand, fighting in Muay Thai and kickboxing bouts to make ends meet.He has previously spoken about the financial realities of that period, when there were no sponsors and fighting was often his only way to pay rent and buy food. He had competed in around 102 or 103 fights across MMA and striking disciplines, including a year in which he fought 25 times in Asia. He even had days when he would turn up at the gym only to be told by his coach that he had a fight that night.Those years also shaped his outlook on fighting. "The hardest part was the beginning of my career, when I had no money and my family probably didn't want me to fight. Thailand was tough as well because you had to fight to make money. Sometimes you were injured, sometimes you were sick, but it didn't matter. You still had to fight."That experience eventually brought him to the UFC. After earning a contract through Dana White's Contender Series in 2023. Since making his UFC debut against Trevin Giles in February 2024, Prates has built a 7-1 record in the promotion. His victories include stoppages of Li Jingliang, Neil Magny, Geoff Neal, former welterweight champion Leon Edwards and former champion Jack Della Maddalena. His only UFC defeat came against Ian Machado Garry in April 2025. He is 24-7 overall, with 19 knockout wins, and has earned a performance bonus for each of his seven UFC victories.The win over Della Maddalena in May 2026 appeared to put Prates in line for a shot at the undisputed welterweight title. He expected to face the two-divison champ Islam Makhachev, but the champion was not ready to compete in January. The UFC instead announced an interim title fight between Prates and unbeaten Ecuadorian Michael Morales for UFC 336 in Toronto on January 30, 2027. The winner is expected to face Makhachev.Prates has not hidden his frustration with the change in plans. He said he had expected the Makhachev fight and was angry that it had not materialised.“He acts like a kid, like an a**h**e,” Prates said, referring to the champion. "I can't do anything about it. I just need to give my best with the opportunity I have now. My opportunity is to become champion against Morales. I'm going to beat Morales, and then I'm going to make Makhachev retire from MMA."Asked whether the situation had given him extra motivation for the Morales fight, Prates was dismissive of the idea. His goal, he said, remained the same: become champion.“No, no, no. It doesn't matter. I just want to be champion. It doesn't matter whether he fights or not, or whether I'm angry or not. My focus is to become champion. I'm working hard for this. Like I said, on January 30, I'll knock Morales out, and then I'll focus on Makhachev,” said Prates.Morales, however, is no straightforward route to that opportunity. The 27-year-old has a perfect professional record of 19-0 and is unbeaten in all seven of his UFC appearances. He has 14 knockout victories overall, and his recent run includes first-round stoppages of Neil Magny, Gilbert Burns and Sean Brady - three established names in the welterweight division.There has also been attention on Morales' size. He remains a welterweight, competing in the 170lb division. But during the India interaction, Prates pointed to the amount of Morales will have to shed before a fight.“He's really strong. He has 100 kilos. He needs to cut 23 kilos to fight. So he's strong. He's young. But I don't know. I think I'm better than him. I have more technique. I have more experience. I'm more handsome than him. I'm smarter,” Prates said.He also conceded that Morales has time on his side and could become champion in the coming years. But Prates does not intend to let that happen at his expense.I think he's going to become a champion soon, maybe in a few years, because he's really young. But now it's my time. I've been working hard for this, and now it's going to be my time. Maybe he'll become champion soon, but right now, it's my turn.Prates has also earned recognition from fellow Brazilian and former light heavyweight champion Alex Pereira, who has named him among the country's fighters worth watching. The two share a friendship, and Prates said Pereira occasionally messages him. He counts Pereira among his favourite fighters to watch.For now, though, his attention is on Morales and the opportunity to win a UFC title. Talk of legacy and what he wants to leave behind can wait. Prates said he still loves competing, even if the training that comes with it has become less appealing after years in the sport.“After these fights, maybe I can think about my legacy, my career, my life,” he said.India, meanwhile, has made a strong first impression. Prates thanked the fans who turned out to meet him and said he would like to return.“Thank you, everybody, for all your support. I'm really enjoying India. I wish I could stay longer, but I'll be back soon.”
Article Summary: Carlos Prates is in India as part of the UFC India Tour. The Brazilian is known for his knockout power inside the Octagon. But he also has a different side to him away from fight night. He enjoys a party, likes spending time with friends and family, and is comfortable striking up conversations.

Article Title: Lionel Messi scripts MLS history! Inter Miami superstar becomes first player to win back-to-back Golden Boots
Article Text:
Inter Miami CF forward Lionel Messi (Image: REUTERS)

Messi's incredible scoring numbers power Inter Miami captain to another Golden Boot

Back-to-back 25-goal seasons put Messi in elite MLS company

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Messi's 43 goal contributions create another MLS milestone

Lionel Messi continues to rewrite the record books in Major League Soccer, with the Inter Miami captain becoming the first player in the league's history to win the Golden Boot in consecutive seasons. At 39, the Argentine superstar showed no signs of slowing down, finishing the 2026 regular season with 26 goals to claim the scoring title for the second year running.Messi finished four goals ahead of FC Dallas forward Petar Musa, who managed 22, while Vancouver Whitecaps FC's Brian White occupied third place with 20 goals. The latest honour also made Messi only the sixth player in MLS history to win the Golden Boot multiple times.In his fourth MLS season, Messi topped the scoring charts despite featuring in just 31 regular-season matches. His 26 goals were accompanied by 17 assists, taking his overall goal contributions to 43 — the third-highest tally recorded in a single MLS season.The Argentine also led the league in goals per game, averaging 0.87, and shared the top spot for the most multi-goal performances with six. He ranked second in goals per 90 minutes, with an impressive average of 0.91.One of the standout aspects of Messi's campaign was his productivity from open play. Of his 26 goals, only one came from the penalty spot, leaving him with 25 non-penalty goals — the second-highest single-season tally in MLS history. The record belongs to Messi himself, who scored 28 non-penalty goals in 2025.Messi's latest Golden Boot further extended his remarkable consistency in front of goal. After scoring 29 times in the 2025 regular season, he became only the second player in MLS history to register at least 25 goals in consecutive campaigns.His dominance has been equally impressive over a longer period. Messi has scored 75 regular-season goals across the last three campaigns, the second-highest tally by any player in a three-season period in MLS history.He is also only the second player, alongside 2023 Golden Boot winner Denis Bouanga, to score at least 20 goals in three consecutive regular seasons.While his goals have grabbed the headlines, Messi's creative influence has been equally significant. His 43 goal contributions in 2026 made him the first player in MLS history to register at least 40 goal contributions in successive seasons.His numbers across the 2024-2026 period underline the scale of his impact. Messi has accumulated 127 goal contributions during these three seasons, comprising goals and assists. That is 28 more than the next-best tally of 98, recorded by Evander over the same period.
Article Summary: Lionel Messi is the first player in Major League Soccer history to win the Golden Boot in consecutive seasons. The Inter Miami captain scored 26 goals in the 2026 regular season to claim the scoring title for the second year running. The 39-year-old is only the sixth player to win Golden Boot multiple times. Messi also led the league in goals per game, averaging 0.87 and shared the top spot for the most multi-goal performances with six.

Article Title: How the Kolkata maidans shaped UP-born Mohammed Shami
Article Text:
Mohammed Shami (PTI Photo)

KOLKATA: Growing up in a small village in Uttar Pradesh’s Amroha district, where life revolved around sugarcane fields and mustard farms, Mohammed Shami ’s rise to international cricket seemed improbable. Yet the son of a farmer somehow defied the odds to become one of India’s greatest fast bowlers.Fast bowling ran in the family. Shami’s elder brother, Haseeb, was known locally for his pace before injuries curtailed his career. Determined to give his son a chance, father Tousif Ahmed sent Shami to train under coach Badruddin Siddique in Moradabad, 22 km from their village of Sahaspur, Alinagar.The road was far from smooth. Shami failed to make Uttar Pradesh age-group teams for three successive years before an unexpected opportunity changed everything.A Kolkata club approached Siddique looking for a fast bowler and the coach immediately recommended his most promising pupil. Within days, a 16-year-old Shami boarded the Punjab Mail to Kolkata.Playing for Dalhousie Athletic Club in the Maidan circuit for Rs 500 a match, Shami soon caught the eye of Town Club official Debabrata Das, who signed him for Rs 70,000 a season and accommodated him at his home.Unlike many modern cricketers, Shami had little interest in gyms or weight training.He preferred running and long bowling spells. His fondness for biryani became legendary in Kolkata’s club circuit, with officials jokingly motivating him with promises of a plate after a match-winning spell.Breaking into Bengal’s senior side remained difficult until then chief selector Sambaran Banerjee spotted him in a local match against Eastern Railway.“I watched him from beside the sightscreen. He took four wickets bowling with the wind. I asked the captain to bring him on against the wind and he took two more. I knew immediately this boy could spearhead India’s attack one day,” Banerjee recalled.What impressed him most was a trait that would later become Shami’s hallmark.“His seam position and release point were exceptional. That very evening I pushed for his inclusion in the Bengal squad.”Shami repaid that faith by claiming three wickets on his Ranji Trophy debut against Assam at Eden Gardens in 2010. Former Bengal captain Manoj Tiwary remembers being struck by his smooth action and natural pace. “He was a lambi race ka ghoda,” Tiwary said.He also points out the influence Wasim Akram had when the Pakistan great joined Kolkata Knight Riders as bowling coach. “Shami wasn’t a regular in the XI initially, but I saw how Akram worked on his game,” Tiwary recalled.
Article Summary: Mohammed Shami is one of India’s greatest fast bowlers. Shami failed to make Uttar Pradesh age-group teams for three successive years. A Kolkata club approached coach Badruddin Siddique looking for a fast bowler and the coach recommended his most promising pupil.

Article Title: Dhruv Jurel, Tilak Varma shine as India A take massive 428-run lead against New Zealand A

India A tightened their grip on the third unofficial Test against New Zealand A after building a commanding 428-run lead on the second day, with Dhruv Jurel, Tilak Varma and Washington Sundar scoring half-centuries on Sunday.Resuming their first innings at 227/2, the hosts continued to pile on the runs, reaching 464/5 before declaring after 146 overs. Jurel led the charge with a 71, while Tilak remained unbeaten on 81 and Washington finished on 50 not out.Jurel, who had resumed on 12, shared a 31-run stand with Tilak before bringing up his half-century off 75 deliveries. He eventually departed for 71 from 95 balls, an innings featuring nine fours and two sixes, after being dismissed by Cameron Paul.Earlier, B Sai Sudharsan could add only 11 runs to his overnight score of 88 before Cameron Gibson bowled him. Tilak then combined with Ravindra Jadeja, who contributed 25, for a 44-run partnership.The left-hander subsequently joined forces with Washington to put India A firmly in control. Their unbeaten 114-run stand took the hosts past the 450-run mark, with Tilak striking five fours and two sixes. Washington also found the boundary twice.New Zealand A had a difficult start to their reply as Prasidh Krishna made an immediate impact on his return to the side following recovery from a left hamstring injury. The fast bowler dismissed openers Rhys Mariu and Curtis Heaphy to leave the visitors at 36/2 at stumps.Dean Foxcroft was unbeaten on 10, while Zak Gibson was batting on one when play ended. New Zealand A still needed 428 runs to catch up with India's first-innings total.
Article Summary: India A build 428-run lead on second day of third unofficial Test against New Zealand A. Dhruv Jurel, Tilak Varma and Washington Sundar all score half- centuries. Article Title: Khushbu's Youth Olympics silver gives Siddi community a new sporting hero
Article Text:
Ex-India goalkeeper Juje Siddi (on the left) and Khushbu Darjada (right) are both Siddis, descendants of East Africans

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

PANAJI: Now based in London, former India goalkeeper Juje Siddi has not been following all that’s happening in Indian sports, but Khushbu Darjada’s silver medal at the Youth Olympics didn’t escape his attention.Darjada took silver in the women’s judo 63kg category in Senegal, the first Olympic medal won by any member of the Siddi community.“This is good news for everyone, particularly the community,” said Juje, the first from the Siddi tribe to represent the country and win gold at the SAFF Championship in 1997. “The feat will motivate so many others from the community to take to sport and win laurels.”Ever since his move to Salgaocar SC in 1994, Juje has stood out for his distinctive look and ‘African’ features. The goalkeeper belongs to the marginalised Siddi community, descendants of East Africans who were brought to India more than five centuries ago. The Siddis have lived in relative seclusion, most on the margins of poverty.“In the 90s, we had good support (from the govt) but now that’s no longer the case. There is private coaching being conducted but coaches are not serious enough. You must prioritise the interest of the community.If the govt steps in, there’s plenty to gain. Siddis are genetically built strong, have great physique and very good in sports,” said the Karwar-born Juje.In 1987, the Sports Authority of India (SAI), spearheaded by the then Union minister of sports Margaret Alva, set up a sports scheme to scout and train members of the community. The Siddi people had athletic abilities, and Juje was among those scouted as part of the Special Area Games (SAG) scheme.He was scouted as an athlete, but when he moved to Bengaluru for schooling, his goalkeeping abilities got noticed. He did well and made it to the India U-16 camp. His selection to the India U-19 team convinced him that he was on the right track.Soon, he was spotted by coach Norbert Gonsalves during a camp in Patiala for Salgaocar.“We were lucky to be part of the SAG scheme. They suddenly stopped the project,” said the goalkeeper.The goalkeeper enjoyed a memorable career with Salgaocar, winning every major trophy in Indian football, including the National Football League in 1999.After his retirement, he took to coaching. Juje had to move to the UK in 2019. Now, at 53, he wants to return and give back to the community that shaped him.
Article Summary: Khushbu Darjada took silver in the women’s judo 63kg category in Senegal. It was the first Olympic medal won by any member of the Siddi community. Former India goalkeeper Juje Siddi is the first Siddi to represent the country and win gold at the SAFF Championship in 1997.

But her promising run came to an end in the WTA 250 Chennai Open quarterfinals after she went down 3-6, 3-6 to American Robin Montgomery here on Friday.Montgomery, a former junior US Open champion, will face defending champion Janice Tjen, who fought back from a set down to beat Polina Kudermetova 5-7, 6-4, 6-2 in the day’s opening last-eight match.The left-handed Montgomery thrives on pace from her opponents and at times looked uncomfortable when Maaya denied her that luxury. A slow, floating backhand first-serve return from 17-year-old Maaya forced the American to generate her own pace, but she could only find the net.Maaya capitalised and went on to break serve, taking a 3-2 lead. Moreover, world No. 151 Montgomery is prone to unforced errors, having committed 59 in her previous match. Maaya, therefore, needed to keep the ball in play and allow the American’s inconsistency to work against her.The Indian failed to do so, as the 21-year-old reeled off the next four games to close out the set in just 38 minutes.Maaya’s first-serve percentage in the opening set was just 52%, and her second serves were not threatening enough.With Montgomery accustomed to playing at the net, she made good use of the volley when required.In the match between Tjen and Polina, the former took charge after losing the opening. Polina had negated Tjen’s preferred backhand slices in the opening set, with the Uzbek constructing the rallies pretty well.However, from there on, she began throwing away points, committing 45 unforced errors, most of which came in the second and third sets. Polina’s inconsistency proved costly.
Article Summary: Maaya Rajeshwaran Revathi loses to Robin Montgomery in the WTA 250 Chennai Open quarterfinals. The 17-year-old wildcard will now face defending champion Janice Tjen. Tjen fought back from a set down to beat Polina Kudermetova in the day’s opening last-eight match.

Article Title: First-timer Jaypal Malviya earns LA28 quota in 10m air pistol
Article Text:
Jaypal Malviya

PUNE: On a day when all eyes on Manu Bhaker to win a medal and a quota place, Jaypal Malviya came unannounced to do the honours at the ISSF World Championships in Doha on Thursday.Madhya Pradesh’s Malviya, who was participating in his first international competition in the medals category, won silver in men’s 10m air pistol event and also booked India's first berth for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.Malviya, 31, scored 242.2 in the final, while China’s Hu Kai shot 243.9 to win gold. Czech Republic’s Jindrich Dubovy took bronze and the third quota place on offer with a score of 220.9.Malviya had entered the final after shooting 585 in the qualification round.Earlier, Manu Bhaker missed on winning a medal and a quota place after finishing fifth in women’s 10m air pistol event. Manu scored 179.9 in the final and a fourth-place finish would have secured at least a quota as there were two Chinese in the top-four and only one athlete from one country gets the quota from one match.Another Indian, Suruchi Singh, met a similar fate as she finished behind Manu with a score of 158.3. Manu had shot 583, while Suruchi had scored 580 to enter the final.In the men’s final, Malviya. the son of a farmer from MP’s Chhindwara district, got off to a modest start with lower 10s and some 9s in between till his first 12 shots. Though he maintained his ranking in the top-5, he changed gears after the 12 shots with 10.6, 10.2, 10.7 and 10.8 to climb up to second position in the 8-shooter final.In the last four rounds, where bronze and gold were decided, Malviya shot two 9.7s and a 10.7 to stay in the hunt, but Kai's 10.6, 10.7 and a 10.5 in the last three shots gave no chance to the Indian for gold.The final had three Chinese shooters, including Paris Games champion Yu Xie and Hu Kai, who had won all the gold medals in the four World Cups last year. The finalists also had Paris Games bronze medallist Paolo Monna of Italy, however, he crashed out of the final at fifth position, while Xie got eliminated at seventh position.“He was playing only in his first international match, that too at the World Championships. He shot really well despite being shaky in the beginning. I feel he controlled his mind well and executed his plan effectively,” India coach and former shooter Samaresh Jung told TOI
Article Summary: Madhya Pradesh's Jaypal Malviya wins silver in men's 10m air pistol event. He also booked India's first berth for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. Earlier, Manu Bhaker missed on winning a medal and a quota place.

Article Title: ‘Everybody can play on turf’: Dutch Olympic champion explains where India are falling behind
Article Text:
Floris Jan Bovelander

Mohali:

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Former Netherlands hockey star Floris jan Bovelander believes India’s vast talent pool can only translate into sustained global success if the country improves access to artificial turf pitches and strengthens grassroots development programmes.In Punjab for the Asian Champions Trophy, Bovelander, who has been involved in hockey development projects in India for more than a decade, said the biggest difference between hockey powers such as the Netherlands and India remained infrastructure at the grassroots level.“We have more than a thousand turf pitches in the Netherlands and all kids start on turf pitches,” Bovelander said. “The techniques and tactics of modern hockey are easier to learn when you play on turf from a young age.”While India possesses a far larger playing base, he noted that many pitches remain concentrated in stadiums and elite centres, limiting access for young players.“You have pitches, but sometimes you’re not allowed to play on them because they’re in stadiums. In the Netherlands, everybody can play on the turf pitches. That’s important for development,” said the two-time Olympic gold medallist.Bovelander, who helped establish the Naval Tata Hockey Academy in Jharkhand and remains involved in community-based programmes through the Bovelander Foundation, stressed that infrastructure alone was not enough.“There is often a lot of focus on high performance, but high-performance hockey benefits from strong grassroots programmes,” he added. “You need festivals, school competitions, youth leagues and good coaching. Elite players inspire young children, but you also need a strong base underneath.”As for the Indian men’s team, Bovelander said it had developed into one of the world’s most difficult sides to beat, citing back-to-back Olympic bronze medals as evidence of its progress. However, he admitted India had occasionally fallen short in key moments at major tournaments.“They are one of the top teams in the world. Maybe they are missing a little bit in the key moments, but they are always there,” he said. “If things go their way at one of the next major tournaments, they can win.”Bovelander also called for a healthy balance between experienced players and emerging talent, saying national teams should avoid relying on reputation alone.“Players should be in the team because of their performances, not because of their history,” he said. “Young players must keep pushing the experienced ones.”India’s 2016 Junior World Cup-winning generation had gone on to form the backbone of the senior side, he noted, but the challenge now was ensuring the next crop of youngsters was given similar opportunities.As far as his discussions with Punjab’s administration is concerned, Bovelander said he hoped to explore ways of contributing to coaching and grassroots initiatives, adding that expanding access to playing facilities would be among the issues he would raise with policymakers.
Article Summary: Former Netherlands hockey star Floris jan Bovelander believes India’s vast talent pool can only translate into sustained global success if the country improves access to artificial turf pitches. He has been involved in hockey development projects in India for more than a decade.

Article Title: Kylian Mbappe creates Champions League history, joins Lionel Messi in elite list
Article Text:
Real Madrid's Kylian Mbappe (AP Photo)

Mbappe milestone as Real Madrid stage comeback against AEK Athens

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Real Madrid forward Kylian Mbappe added another milestone to his impressive UEFA Champions League career on Wednesday, becoming the second-fastest player to register 100 goal contributions in the competition's history.The French superstar reached the landmark during Real Madrid's clash against AEK Athens, finding the net in the 78th minute to take his combined tally of goals and assists to 100. Mbappe has now recorded 74 goals and 26 assists in 102 Champions League appearances.Only Lionel Messi reached the milestone quicker, taking 101 matches to register 100 goal contributions. The Argentina great achieved the feat while representing Barcelona and Paris Saint-Germain (PSG) before moving to Major League Soccer (MLS), where he currently plays for Inter Miami.Cristiano Ronaldo remains at the top of the all-time Champions League goal contributions chart with 182, comprising 140 goals and 42 assists.The record-breaking moment came during an eventful encounter in Athens, where Real Madrid had to fight back after falling behind twice before eventually securing a 3-2 victory.AEK Athens made an early breakthrough through Aboubakary Koita, who opened the scoring in the 12th minute following an assist from Luka Jovic.Real Madrid thought they had found an equaliser when Vinicius Jr 's cross ended up in the net following a touch from Jude Bellingham. However, the goal was ruled out because the English midfielder was adjudged to be offside.Bellingham made up for the disallowed effort just three minutes later, producing an excellent backheel finish in the 32nd minute to bring Madrid back into the contest, as reported by Goal.com.Mbappe also had an opportunity to create danger when he picked out an unmarked Marc Cucurella, but the latter failed to make the most of the chance with his weaker foot.The hosts regained the advantage in the 75th minute, with Koita turning provider this time by setting up Stavro Pilo, who put AEK Athens on the verge of a memorable victory.However, Madrid responded almost immediately. Denzel Dumfries delivered a cross that Mbappe converted in the 78th minute, restoring parity while simultaneously bringing up his 100th Champions League goal contribution.With the match heading towards its conclusion, Federico Valverde stepped up with a stunning strike, finding the top corner to complete Madrid's comeback and seal a dramatic 3-2 win.The victory ensured that Mbappe's personal milestone was accompanied by another important result for Real Madrid in Europe.
Article Summary: Kylian Mbappe becomes second-fastest player to register 100 Champions League goal contributions. The French forward reached the landmark during Real Madrid's 3-2 win against AEK Athens on Wednesday. Only Lionel Messi reached the milestone quicker, taking 101 matches to do so.

For a league that has spent decades turning basketball players into global icons and team jerseys into fashion statements, the NBA 's ambitions in India were never going to be restricted to television screens. The challenge, however, is turning that appeal into a sustainable business.India, with its young population, expanding digital audience and growing appetite for global sports and entertainment, represents a significant long-term opportunity for the league. But the NBA is conscious that building a presence in a cricket-dominated market requires more than securing a broadcaster and hoping fans tune in to watch games played thousands of kilometres and many timezones away.It is looking to create multiple entry points for consumers, with basketball, fashion, music, entertainment and retail forming parts of a larger commercial strategy.The latest step in that direction is the expansion of its merchandising partnership with Indian apparel company Suditi. Having worked together since 2018, the two have extended their association, with Suditi taking over the operation of NBAStore.in in October 2026.The expanded portfolio includes casual shirts and lifestyle footwear, alongside jerseys, T-shirts, jackets, sweatshirts, headwear and accessories.More significantly, the partnership will see the NBA open its first physical store in India in 2027. It is an important development for a league looking to take its relationship with fans beyond digital engagement and into everyday consumption.The idea is to make NBA merchandise a lifestyle proposition rather than limit it to conventional sports apparel. Its teams, players and iconic jerseys already have recognition beyond basketball-following circles. Just look at numerous LA Lakers, Chicago Bulls, Michael Jordan, Steph Curry, LeBron James knockoffs that get sold in the local markets. The opportunity lies in converting that cultural appeal into official merchandise sales.Long-term commercial partnerships are another important part of the NBA's business model. Swiss watchmaker Tissot, which has been associated with the league for a decade, is an example of how these relationships can evolve beyond brand visibility."Our partnerships are built on shared values, a common vision and a commitment to evolving together. The decade-long NBA association exemplifies this, with both brands continually innovating to enhance fan experience, most recently through a redesigned shot clock now adopted across the WNBA," Tissot CEO Sylvain Dolla told TimesofIndia.com.Dolla added that the same approach extended to the brand's associations across basketball, cycling and motorsport, where it works with Swiss Timing to develop sport-specific solutions. "Our objective is to contribute to each sport's growth through long-term collaboration and innovation," he added.But retail and partnerships are only part of the equation.The NBA has spent considerable time experimenting with how Indian audiences consume its product. Its broadcast journey has included a decade-long association with Sony, followed by partnerships with MTV and digital platforms. It also explored making 100 games available live on YouTube, while its three-year association with Prasar Bharati took basketball content to DD Sports and a wider free-to-air audience.The reasoning was straightforward: live games alone cannot drive growth in a market where matches are played at inconvenient hours for Indian viewers."You can't just focus on broadcast and say, 'please watch my game.' You have to do other things around the sport," said Rajah Chaudhry, NBA's Asia-Pacific head of strategy, during an interaction with TimesofIndia.com in June."The objective is not to get cocooned into just one way of saying that live games are the way to be. We want to try different ways because people like to consume games in different ways in the country. That's our objective," added Sunny Malik, NBA India's Country Head.For the 2026-27 season, NBA games are available live in India on Prime Video and NBA League Pass. The challenge is to ensure that audiences remain connected to the league even when they are not watching live action.That is where digital content assumes importance. The NBA's Indian social media platforms have accumulated more than eight million followers, generating over 1.8 billion impressions and 1.35 billion video views. Highlights, short-form clips, player stories and locally produced content allow the league to remain part of the conversation throughout the year.Its approach to fan engagement also extends beyond the screen.BUDX NBA House, which moved from Mumbai to New Delhi in May this year, brings basketball together with music, fashion, celebrity appearances and entertainment. The format is particularly relevant in India, where the NBA's cultural appeal can reach audiences who may not necessarily follow the sport closely.The initiative has also found relevance beyond India, with elements of the experience informing the league's approach in other Asia-Pacific markets.There is, however, a distinction between building awareness and building a business. Social media numbers and event attendance offer encouraging signs, but converting occasional engagement into regular viewership, merchandise sales and long-term commercial partnerships remains the bigger test.Cricket continues to command the country's sporting attention, sponsorship money and broadcast market. The NBA also has to contend with a time-zone disadvantage and the challenge of developing a sizeable paying audience for a sport that still occupies a relatively small space in India's domestic sporting landscape.The league's India strategy, therefore, is built around connecting several businesses rather than relying on one. Broadcast distribution creates visibility, digital content sustains engagement, live experiences build communities, while merchandise and retail offer opportunities to monetise that relationship.The pieces are gradually falling into place. The question is whether they can come together to create something bigger.For the NBA, India's opportunity is not merely about getting more people to watch basketball. It is about making the league part of their sporting, cultural and consumer lives.
Article Summary: The NBA is expanding its merchandising partnership with Indian apparel company Suditi. The partnership will see the NBA open its first physical store in India in 2027. It is an important development for a league looking to take its relationship with fans beyond digital engagement and into everyday consumption.

Article Title: ‘He got greedy’: Ex-India captain's blunt take on Arshdeep Singh after four-wicket haul
Article Text:
India bowler Arshdeep Singh celebrates with teammate Virat Kohli (AP/PTI)

Jadeja impressed with Anshul Kamboj

Former India cricketer Ajay Jadeja has praised Arshdeep Singh's overall performance in India's five-wicket victory over New Zealand in the first ODI in Auckland, but believes the left-arm pacer could have avoided an expensive finish to his spell.India began their five-match ODI series with a comfortable win at Eden Park on Wednesday, November 4. In a rain-interrupted contest reduced to 32 overs per side, New Zealand were bowled out for 185 before India chased down the revised target of 143 in just 22.4 overs. Virat Kohli led the chase with a fluent 74, while Shubman Gill contributed 37 as the duo stitched together a 113-run partnership. India eventually crossed the finish line with five wickets to spare and 56 deliveries remaining.With the ball, Arshdeep was India's leading wicket-taker, claiming four wickets in his 10 overs. However, his figures of 4/70 were inflated by an expensive final over in which New Zealand tailender Blair Tickner struck him for three sixes, taking 23 runs off the over.Assessing the pacer's performance, Jadeja felt Arshdeep had been impressive for most of his spell but allowed the opportunity to complete a five-wicket haul to influence his bowling towards the end."I would call him slightly greedy. He himself said that as well. If you remove his last over, he had dismissed four batters before that and had given 40-odd runs. He got slightly greedy for the fifth wicket in the last over," Jadeja said on Sony Sports Network.Arshdeep had himself admitted after the match that the fifth wicket would have been his favourite, indicating that he was keen to complete a five-wicket haul. Despite missing out on the milestone, his four-wicket effort placed him in an exclusive group of Indian fast bowlers to achieve the feat in an ODI in New Zealand, alongside Javagal Srinath and Mohammed Shami.Jadeja, however, stressed that the expensive final over should not overshadow what Arshdeep brings to India's bowling combination. He pointed to the value of having a left-arm fast bowler in an attack that already features Jasprit Bumrah, adding that the competition for places would only benefit the team."It happens. It's natural, but Arshdeep Singh is showing that he can play in ODIs as well, which I believe is a very good thing when a left-arm seamer gets added to this attack with (Jasprit) Bumrah. The competition has increased a lot, which is very good for India," Jadeja elaborated.Jadeja also reserved praise for Anshul Kamboj, who delivered an economical spell of 2/22 from his 10 overs and walked away with the Player of the Match award.The former India batter acknowledged that Kamboj had faced questions over his bowling during his Test debut against England in 2025, particularly regarding his pace and tendency to bowl no-balls. However, he felt the youngster had shown considerable improvement in Auckland.Jadeja also suggested that Kamboj's workload before the England assignment could have contributed to his struggles, pointing out that fatigue can affect a bowler's execution. His performance against New Zealand, according to Jadeja, reflected better pace, consistency and accuracy."He bowled extremely well. The vision everyone had was that he didn't have pace when he played in England and was bowling a lot of no-balls. I think he had come after playing a lot of cricket then. So a guy also gets tired. It's not that easy. Then he was playing for the first time, but the consistency and the slight increase in his pace he showed today (Wednesday), if we talk about the accuracy amongst the four bowlers, it's Anshul Kamboj," Jadeja added.
Article Summary: India beat New Zealand by five wickets in the first ODI in Auckland. Ajay Jadeja praised Arshdeep Singh's performance, but said he could have avoided expensive final over. Jadeja also praised Anshul Kamboj's bowling, saying he had shown improvement.

Article Title: Late release, upright seam, heavy ball: Decoding Mohammed Shami’s sorcery
Article Text:
Mohammed Shami

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Few bowlers possessed the ability to strip a batter of his technique, judgement, and ego like Mohammed Shami . The fast bowler from a nondescript village in Uttar Pradesh’s Sahaspur, which literally translates to the “land of courage”, bowled with a big heart, indefatigable spirit, and unmatched skill over 64 Tests.Former England captain Alastair Cook’s dismissal during the Visakhapatnam Test in 2016 was a case in point. Shami bowled a series of outswingers that forced Cook to play away from his body. On cue, he then delivered a perfect inswinger that jagged back sharply to sneak past Cook's defence and cannon onto the stumps.“It’s all in those beautiful wrists,” Shami’s childhood coach Badruddin Siddiqui told TOI.“The reason for his success was that he released the ball late and did not rush through his action. This helped him extract late swing off the track. With those malleable wrists, he made subtle changes at the point of release that batters found hard to pick,” the coach demystified Shami’s skill set.Like S Sreesanth, Shami possessed one of the most upright, God-gifted seam positions in world cricket. Shami was also a bit of a paradox because of the ability to make the old ball skid low while also hurling the ‘heavy ball’ that flew past the batter’s nose.The ‘heavy ball’ — the delivery that pitches shorter and reaches the batter quicker than expected, and hits the bat with extra force despite bowling from a relatively smooth, upright run-up — became Shami’s calling card on numerous overseas tours.The 2018 Johannesburg Test was a classic example: he dismantled South Africa, cruising at 124/1, for 177 to hand India a landmark 63-run win. Shami finished with figures of 5/28, unleashing his trademark ‘heavy ball’ on the spicy Wanderers pitch.At times, he could be erratic even when the conditions were loaded in his favour. But without any warning, he would return with a magical, match-altering spell against the run of play. This streak of unpredictability made Shami irresistible, and it was instrumental in India winning more matches abroad, especially under Virat Kohli ’s captaincy.Shami was also a great senior, who passed on his art and tricks of the trade to youngsters.“I learnt a lot of things from him during my time in the IPL. Subtle things like bowling at the death and with the semi-new ball,” Uttar Pradesh pacer Ankit Rajput said.At 36, Shami had been performing admirably in this Ranji season, picking up 14 wickets in his last three games. Yet, the constant snubs and time away from international cricket had hurt him.“He was trying hard to make a comeback. But after a point, he realised he was not going to get another chance in Tests, which is why he chose to retire,” Badruddin explained.“He wants to play the ODI World Cup next year. He has kept that window open,” he added. Shami is India’s highest wicket-taker in the 50-over World Cups, with 55 scalps from 18 games at an impressive average of 13.5.The sorcerer of seam signs off from Tests, leaving a gaping hole in India’s bowling roster. Finding Shami’s replacement would be as difficult as locating Sahaspur on the India map.
Article Summary: Mohammed Shami has announced his retirement from international cricket. The 36-year-old bowled with a big heart, indefatigable spirit, and unmatched skill over 64 Tests. He is India’s highest wicket-taker in the 50-over World Cups, with 55 scalps from 18 games at an impressive average of 13.5.

Article Title: ‘I will let my bat do the talking’: Mukul Choudhary on handling pressure, absorbing advice at LSG
Article Text:
Mukul Choudhary

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

JAIPUR: Mukul Choudhary isn’t one to dwell on selection twists. The 22-year-old wicketkeeper-batter from Jhunjhunu has this season endured a turbulent domestic campaign marked by bizarre selection calls. After an ankle injury saw Sumit Godara replace him in the first game, a fully fit Mukul was entirely omitted from Rajasthan’s second Ranji Trophy match. The shuffling peaked when he was named for the third match, only to be abruptly replaced by Vishal Harsh the next day and relegated to the Under-23 setup.True to form, the Lucknow Super Giants (LSG) finisher responded emphatically, smashing 112 off 129 balls against Mumbai in his first CK Nayudu Trophy game. He was then handed the U-23 captaincy after original skipper Himanshu Nehra was promoted to the senior squad, only for the selection dynamics to pivot again on Saturday with his own inclusion into Rajasthan’s T20 squad for the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy.After leading the U-23 side to an outright victory over Bihar on Friday, Mukul is now home for Diwali. In a candid chat with TOI, the youngster reflects on his whirlwind journey, tactical growth, and an off-season developmental stint in the UK, remaining focused on letting his bat do the talking.Mukul admits he never anticipated fetching a massive deal of Rs 2.6 crore. “I never thought I’d command such a price tag,” he says. “My domestic season was going well, and after performing in the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy 2025-26, my confidence grew. A couple of franchises, specifically MI and RCB, called me for trials. So while I knew some team might pick me, I certainly didn’t expect to secure such a substantial contract. ”Interestingly, his path to LSG was entirely unpredictable. “LSG didn’t hold trials for me. There was no prior contact or discussion,” Mukul reveals. “I didn’t even realize I was on their radar, let alone expect to join them.”Breaking into the playing XI required treating internal practice matches like qualifiers. “When I joined, there was an open slot in the middle order,” he shares. “Our batting coach was Lance Klusener and he told me directly: ‘For you, the practice matches are your selection matches. Play them with that mindset if you want to make the final XI.’ I was the highest run-scorer across all three practice matches, even won one game single-handedly. That paved my way into the side, which is no small feat for an uncapped player.”The road wasn’t smooth. Recalling early missed opportunities, Mukul says, “I was dismissed for just 16 in my first game, and in the next match, I missed two or three full tosses. Even though we won, I went back to my hotel room feeling completely dejected. At this level, you rarely get second chances.”A critical turning point came right before a crucial clash against Kolkata Knight Riders, a match where he would go on to smash an unbeaten 27-ball 54, including seven sixes. In the lead-up to the game, the then LSG skipper Rishabh Pant noticed him batting too cautiously in the nets.“I was batting quite defensively,” Mukul remembers. “Rishabh bhai noticed it and intervened. He told me, ‘What are you doing? Express yourself and play your natural game... We believe in you, you will get your opportunities, and you have to back yourself to deliver.’ Later, on the team bus, he called me over and reinforced that confidence.”That dugout backing allowed him to play with complete freedom, contributing to a famous win.Addressing his tactical progress, Mukul keeps his cards close to his chest. “I won’t share all the technical details,” Mukul smiles. “There are a couple of finisher-role specifics I am adding, figuring out how to develop even better scoring shots that can help the team when it matters most.”Once the IPL season concluded, LSG arranged for him to travel to the UK, where the coaching staff, including Justin Langer, ran camps in Manchester. “The UK experience was great because the wickets are different, and pace bowlers get more help there,” he notes. “Adapting to those conditions helped refine my game.”To maintain momentum, Mukul regularly trains at the Coaching Beyond Academy in Chennai under former India bowling coach Bharat Arun and G Jaikumar, the newly appointed batting coach for LSG. “Working under minds like Bharat Arun sir and Jaikumar sir at the Chennai academy has been incredible for my development,” Mukul adds.Whether talking about his domestic grind or shifting formats, Mukul’s focus remains singular. “Be it LSG or Rajasthan, or red-ball or white-ball, the goal is to win matches for the team. You cannot let success alter your intensity. I just want to keep scoring runs, prove myself every single day, and let the bat do the talking,” the youngster says.
Article Summary: Mukul Choudhary has endured a turbulent domestic campaign. The 22-year-old wicketkeeper-batter from Jhunjhunu has endured bizarre selection calls. The Lucknow Super Giants (LSG) finisher smashed 112 off 129 balls against Mumbai. Mukul admits he never anticipated fetching a massive deal of Rs 2.6 crore.

Article Title: ‘Wrong to eliminate toss in U-23 matches’: Dilip Vengsarkar urges BCCI to restore it
Article Text:
Dilip Vengsarkar

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

MUMBAI: Former India captain Dilip Vengsarkar has criticised the BCCI ’s decision to scrap the toss in the Col CK Nayudu Trophy for the past two seasons, urging the board to restore the practice from next season. In May 2024, then BCCI secretary Jay Shah announced that the toss would be done away with in the men’s under-23 tournament for the 2024-25 season, with the visiting team given the choice of batting or bowling first.The move was aimed at curbing the practice of home teams preparing spin-friendly pitches to gain an advantage. The BCCI’s move was the first instance of the toss being scrapped in Indian domestic cricket. The England and Wales Cricket Board had also done away with it in the County Championship from 2016 to 2019, before restoring it in 2020.“It’s absolutely wrong to do away with the toss in U-23 matches. The element of toss brings a different charm and excitement to a cricket match,” Vengsarkar told TOI.Vengsarkar said that teams must learn to adapt to different conditions. “The wicket and conditions are the same for both teams. If you play a balanced team, you can cope with any conditions. And what happens if you make a wicket to suit your strength, but lose the toss? A toss adds a different, but necessary dimension to a cricket game,” he said.“Sometimes, when you are not sure about whether to bat or bowl first, it could be a good toss to lose. The BCCI should reintroduce the toss in its U-23 tournament from the next season. There’s no question about it,” he added.

In May 2024, then BCCI secretary Jay Shah announced that the toss would be done away with in the men’s under-23 tournament for the 2024-25 season. The move was aimed at curbing the practice of home teams preparing spin-friendly pitches to gain an advantage.

Article Title: ‘I haven’t thrown anyone under the bus’: Usman Khawaja hits back amid Sandpapergate row
Article Text:
Australia's Usman Khawaja (AP Photo/James Elsby)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The Sandpapergate scandal that rocked Australian cricket in 2018 has returned to the spotlight following fresh revelations from Usman Khawaja , who has claimed that the entire team was aware of the ball-tampering attempts during the Test series against South Africa.Excerpts from Khawaja's upcoming autobiography, Sabr, published by the Sydney Morning Herald (SMH) on Saturday, suggested that the controversial practice was not restricted to the third Test in Cape Town but had also been attempted in the preceding match. The revelations have triggered strong reactions, with former Australia coach Darren Lehmann rejecting Khawaja's claims and ex-England captain Michael Vaughan also expressing his displeasure.Amid the growing controversy, Khawaja took to social media on Sunday to clarify his comments, insisting that his account had been misrepresented and that he stood by what he had written.“Alright, it’s time to clear up some facts because the media has taken this to the moon, as expected.“I stayed quiet yesterday, but number one, if you read my article, you would have seen when I mentioned it was all of us that’s implying that, whether we like it or not, we are all responsible for what happened.Together, as a team, we need to take that collectively. That is all,” the former Australian batter said.However, Khawaja stopped short of retracting his assertion that the players knew about the ball-tampering episode.“But now that everyone’s talking, am I going to deny that everyone knew? Nah. I won’t deny that either.“But I never speak on behalf of anyone else in my book. Contrary to all the headlines the clickbait media would have you think. Don’t get caught up in this s***.”The former opener also addressed suggestions that he had chosen to make the revelations eight years after the incident to generate publicity and boost sales of his autobiography. Khawaja maintained that he had deliberately held back the account until the Australian team had returned from South Africa."What I say now isn’t a reflection of them anymore, and now my words don’t influence the team at all. I speak for myself.“But even so, I refused to publish any of this while the boys were still in South Africa. That’s why I called Pat (Cummins).“Why would someone who really wants to increase the sale of his book refuse the greatest marketing opportunity he has? I haven’t thrown anyone under the bus... those three guys [Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft] who took the blame for all of us, they’re the victims,” he said.Khawaja reveals two teammates opposed collective responsibilityFurther details from the autobiography, reported by Code Sports, have also shed light on a disagreement within the Australian dressing room after the Cape Town Test. Khawaja claimed that two members of the team objected to his proposal that the players collectively accept responsibility for what had happened.“This was the most disappointing thing for me. I knew who those two guys were, and it was ludicrous; out of everyone, it was them. It showed me their true colours, though. When the going got tough, all they cared about was themselves. But I was not going to stop fighting this cause,” Khawaja wrote.The issue resurfaced years later when Cameron Bancroft appeared to suggest in an interview that Australia's bowlers had knowledge of the ball-tampering operation.Following those remarks, Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc and Nathan Lyon issued a joint statement distancing themselves from the incident.Khawaja's autobiography further claims that he contacted then head coach Justin Langer and CEO Todd Greenberg after Bancroft's interview. He reportedly urged them to ensure that the entire team accepted responsibility rather than placing the burden solely on the bowling group.According to Khawaja, both Langer and Greenberg agreed with his suggestion. However, the eventual statement released publicly came only from the four Australian bowlers, leaving the former batter disappointed with how the matter was handled.The latest revelations have reopened questions surrounding one of the darkest episodes in Australian cricket, with Khawaja maintaining that responsibility for the incident extended beyond the three players who were formally punished.
Article Summary: Usman Khawaja claims that the entire team was aware of ball-tampering attempts during the Test series against South Africa. The revelations have triggered strong reactions, with former Australia coach Darren Lehmann and ex-England captain Michael Vaughan also expressing their displeasure. The former Australian batter maintains that responsibility for the incident extended beyond the three players who were formally punished.

As tributes poured in from former players, fans and the BCCI after Mohammed Shami announced his retirement from Test cricket on Friday, they all pointed to the same truth: India had bid farewell to one of its finest pacers.Over 13 years, Shami played 64 Tests, claimed 229 wickets and helped transform India’s pace-bowling identity. Amid the praise, though, lingered uncomfortable questions: Was he valued enough in the final phase of his career?Like several senior Indian cricketers before him, Shami’s Test journey ended not on a cricket field but through a social media post. There was no farewell Test among passionate fans in a full stadium. For a bowler who had such a massive impact on India’s fortunes, the ending felt understated and incomplete.Former India coach Ravi Shastri voiced that sentiment forcefully. “Without him, the fast-bowling unit would not have functioned,” Shastri said on Sony Sports Network during the second ODI in Wellington on Saturday.The former coach was convinced Shami still had plenty left to offer. “I definitely thought he had another 30-40 wickets left in him.He should have played in the last 12 months and should have played Tests here.”Former India bowling coach Paras Mhambrey shared a similar view.“Personally, I would have loved to see him represent India again, in Test cricket and in other formats as well,” Mhambrey told TOI. “He’s played Ranji Trophy and Duleep Trophy, done well and, honestly, he’s a joy to watch. He makes everything look so easy.”Mhambrey stopped short of questioning the decision-makers, though, acknowledging that outsiders were unaware of the conversations that may have taken place between Shami, the selectors and the team management.Shastri’s strongest criticism, however, was reserved for the repeated doubts over Shami’s fitness despite his performances for Bengal in domestic cricket.“He was bowling 15 to 20 overs daily. What else do you want a player to do to prove his fitness?” Shastri asked.Shami’s final Test came in the World Test Championship final against Australia at The Oval in June 2023. For a bowler who continued to play domestic cricket thereafter, it felt like a forced full stop.Ask Mhambrey what made Shami special and the answer arrives quickly.“Very few bowlers in world cricket had that kind of upright seam presentation. As a batter, you never knew whether the ball would come in or go away. He kept asking questions every ball.”That seam position became Shami’s trademark. Few bowlers of his generation attacked the stumps as relentlessly. Of his 229 Test wickets, 101 came through bowled or lbw dismissals.Mhambrey believes another underrated aspect of Shami’s success was his simplicity.“He wasn’t data-driven. He kept things very simple. He knew what he wanted and how he wanted to prepare. There wasn’t too much noise around his process.”The numbers underline just how valuable he was. On spin-friendly home surfaces, where fast bowlers often played supporting roles, Shami remained a match-winner. He claimed 76 wickets in India at an extraordinary average of 22, and India did not lose any of the 21 home Tests in which he featured.Part of that success stemmed from a quality often overlooked.“He surprised people with his pace,” Mhambrey said. “He was much quicker than batters felt. He had great rhythm and could replicate it again and again. That’s why you saw so many bowled and lbw dismissals.”Few teammates enjoyed facing him in the nets. Dinesh Karthik once described the experience as “torture”, while Shami’s fierce practice battles with Virat Kohli could have been part of many highlight reels.For Shami, bowling was never a chore. It was romance.During the Covid lockdown, he returned to his farmhouse in Amroha, built clay practice tracks and spent hours bowling and running to stay sharp. That old-school philosophy, Mhambrey believes, defined an entire generation of Indian fast bowlers.“Shami, Bumrah, Ishant, Umesh, Bhuvneshwar, they bowled a lot. Skill came first. Fitness supplemented that skill. If you want control, you need to bowl. If you want to know your limits, you need to bowl.”Perhaps that is why Shami earned the label “Second-Innings Shami”, a bowler whose threat often intensified as matches wore on. Mhambrey observes that his pace rarely dipped, his accuracy remained relentless and his upright seam challenged both edges of quality batters.Which makes it all the more ironic that he was never afforded a second innings in his own Test career.“In this 13-year journey, this cap and this ball made me Mohammed Shami,” he said in his farewell message. “I did fall, I did get hurt, I did get injured. But I stood up again for this badge.”For that, Shami deserved one final opportunity to walk away on his own terms, but he probably retired hurt.Mohammed Shami’s rare blend of pace, seam movement and relentless accuracy made him a match-winner.revisits five of his finest Test spells...
Article Summary: Mohammed Shami announced his retirement from Test cricket on Friday. Over 13 years, Shami played 64 Tests, claimed 229 wickets and helped transform India’s pace-bowling identity. Tributes poured in from former players, fans and the BCCI.

Gurnoor Brar produced a memorable performance with the ball in the second ODI against New Zealand, registering the second-best bowling figures by an Indian fast bowler in ODIs in New Zealand. Article Title: ‘There was nothing wrong’: Sunil Gavaskar shuts down criticism of Gautam Gambhir's decision to bat Axar Patel at No. 5

Legendary India batter Sunil Gavaskar has backed the team management's decision to promote Axar Patel ahead of KL Rahul in the second ODI against New Zealand, explaining the tactical thinking behind the move despite the all-rounder's failure with the bat.India were chasing a modest target of 135 at Hnry Stadium in Wellington but found themselves in early trouble against New Zealand's disciplined pace attack. After losing Shubman Gill, Virat Kohli and Rohit Sharma, the visitors slipped to 39/3. Axar was then sent in at No. 5, ahead of Rahul , but could manage only seven runs before falling, leaving India struggling at 47/4.The decision by head coach Gautam Gambhir and captain Gill to push Axar up the order attracted criticism from sections of fans and experts. However, Gavaskar felt there was sound reasoning behind the move, particularly the advantage of disrupting a bowling attack's plans by introducing a left-handed batter."The bowlers have slight difficulty if a left-handed batter comes because you have to change the line and length you would have for a right-hander. In trying to do that, your line can change slightly even to the right-hander, where more chances of getting runs are created," Gavaskar explained, speaking on Sony Sports network after the game.The former India captain also pointed out that such tactical decisions should not be judged solely by their outcome, as they can produce different results on different occasions."There was nothing wrong with that thought process. If Axar had scored runs, you would have said how good the captaincy was. Such moves work at times and don't work on other occasions, and it didn't work this time. You also knew there was a solid player like Rahul after him. That's why you experiment at times," he added.Axar's promotion was not an entirely unfamiliar move for India. The left-hander has previously been trusted with a higher batting position in important matches, most notably during the 2024 T20 World Cup final, when he forged a crucial partnership with Virat Kohli.He also occupied the No. 5 position ahead of Rahul throughout India's victorious Champions Trophy 2025 campaign.In Wellington, however, it was Rahul who eventually took responsibility for keeping India's chase on track. After walking in following Axar's dismissal, he combined with Shreyas Iyer, who contributed 30 off 46 deliveries, to steady the innings.Rahul was cautious initially, playing 18 dot balls in his first 20 deliveries before finding opportunities to accelerate. He remained unbeaten on 26 when rain stopped play, with India at 113/7 after 26 overs.India were four runs ahead of the DLS par score of 109 when the match was abandoned, handing the visitors a four-wicket victory and a 2-0 lead in the five-match series.The win was set up by an impressive performance from India's young pace attack. Gurnoor Brar claimed career-best figures of 4/30, while Auqib Nabi and Anshul Kamboj picked up two wickets apiece to dismiss New Zealand for 134 in 41 overs.Daryl Mitchell top-scored for the hosts with 55, but New Zealand's total proved insufficient as India secured another DLS victory in the series.
Article Summary: Sunil Gavaskar backs India's decision to promote Axar Patel ahead of KL Rahul in the second ODI against New Zealand. India were chasing a modest target of 135 at Hnry Stadium in Wellington. The decision by head coach Gautam Gambhir and captain Gill to push Axar up the order attracted criticism from sections of fans and experts.

Article Title: Slippery turf, testing conditions: KL Rahul keeps his cool as India take 2-0 series lead against New Zealand
Article Text:
India and New Zealand players after the 2nd ODI. (AP/PTI Photo)

It has been a while since bowlers dominated a white-ball series quite so emphatically, putting batters under pressure and dictating terms. In an era of 350-plus totals and 300-run chases, these low-scoring contests have been a refreshing reminder that tight bowling, rather than brute-force batting, can make for compelling cricket.India’s star-studded batting lineup was blown away by New Zealand’s pacers before a composed KL Rahul produced a vital, unbeaten 26 off 38 balls, including two sixes and two fours, to guide the visitors to a hard-fought four-run win via the DLS method in a rain-affected second ODI in Wellington on Thursday. Rahul, aided by vice-captain Shreyas Iyer’s 30 off 46 balls and veteran opener Rohit Sharma’s 23 off 28, made sure India’s young fast bowlers were rewarded for their excellent work. Gurnoor Brar was the standout, returning career-best figures of four for 30 in his 10 overs.India now lead the five-match series 2-0 and will have a chance to seal it in the third ODI in Hamilton on Tuesday. Chasing 135 in 47 overs, they were in trouble at 113 for seven after 26 overs, still needing 22 with three wickets in hand, when rain returned. With the DLS par score at 109 at that point, India edged home.Brar was India’s standout performer, using his height to extract steep bounce and operating with raw pace and aggression. He removed Tom Latham (7), Glenn Phillips (0), Mitchell Santner (31) and Nathan Smith (3).The tall Punjab pacer found strong support from Auqib Nabi, who took two for 31 in seven overs, and Anshul Kamboj, who returned two for 25 in eight. The three seamers shared eight wickets as India bowled New Zealand out for 134 in 41 overs, making full use of the pace, bounce and movement on offer.India were never going to find the chase easy on such a surface, but the task proved tougher than expected. Skipper Shubman Gill fell for a rare first-ball duck, caught at second slip by Henry Nicholls off Jacob Duffy in the second over. Duffy struck again when Virat Kohli drove uppishly to short cover, leaving India 17/2.Rohit lived dangerously after being dropped by Nathan Smith at deep backward square leg, but briefly counterattacked with his trademark pull shots, hitting Kyle Jamieson for two sixes. Axar Patel, promoted to No. 5, struggled for timing before ramping Matthew Fisher to deep backward point for 7 off 17 balls, leaving India 47 for four in the 13th over.Shreyas played a few attractive strokes but once again fell to the short ball, with Jamieson dismissing him for 30. At 86 for five, India were in trouble before Rahul steadied the innings. He produced some of the shots of the match, pulling Smith for a four and a six in the 16th over before dispatching Jamieson for another six in the 23rd. India lost Naman Dhir (12) and Kamboj (1) late, but Rahul’s calm presence kept them ahead of the DLS mark.Earlier, playing his third ODI, Nabi claimed his maiden international wicket when Tim Seifert was caught by Kamboj at mid-wicket for a duck. He then removed Will Young (11), who edged a fine delivery to Rahul. Kamboj had Nicholls playing on before Brar struck twice in the 20th over, dismissing Latham and Phillips with short-pitched deliveries.Axar also impressed, taking 2/28 in nine overs, including the key wicket of Daryl Mitchell, who made a fighting 55 off 104 balls.
Article Summary: India beat New Zealand by four runs in second ODI in Wellington. India bowled New Zealand out for 134 in 41 overs. Gurnoor Brar was the standout, returning career-best figures of four for 30 in his 10 overs. India now lead the five- match series 2-0.

Article Title: Late release, upright seam, heavy ball: Decoding Mohammed Shami's sorcery
Article Text:
Mohammed Shami (File Photo)

.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Few bowlers possessed the ability to strip a batter of his technique, judgement, and ego like Mohammed Shami . The fast bowler from a nondescript village in Uttar Pradesh’s Sahaspur, which literally translates to the “land of courage”, bowled with a big heart, indefatigable spirit, and unmatched skill over 64 Tests.Former England captain Alastair Cook’s dismissal during the Visakhapatnam Test in 2016 was a case in point. Shami bowled a series of outswingers that forced Cook to play away from his body. On cue, he then delivered a perfect inswinger that jagged back sharply to sneak past Cook's defence and cannon onto the stumps.“It’s all in those beautiful wrists,” Shami’s childhood coach Badruddin Siddiqui told TOI“The reason for his success was that he released the ball late and did not rush through his action. This helped him extract late swing off the track. With those malleable wrists, he made subtle changes at the point of release that batters found hard to pick,” the coach demystified Shami’s skill set.Like S Sreesanth, Shami possessed one of the most upright, God-gifted seam positions in world cricket. Shami was also a bit of a paradox because of the ability to make the old ball skid low while also hurling the ‘heavy ball’ that flew past the batter’s nose.The ‘heavy ball’ — the delivery that pitches shorter and reaches the batter quicker than expected, and hits the bat with extra force despite bowling from a relatively smooth, upright run-up — became Shami’s calling card on numerous overseas tours.The 2018 Johannesburg Test was a classic example: he dismantled South Africa, cruising at 124/1, for 177 to hand India a landmark 63-run win. Shami finished with figures of 5/28, unleashing his trademark ‘heavy ball’ on the spicy Wanderers pitch.At times, he could be erratic even when the conditions were loaded in his favour. But without any warning, he would return with a magical, match-altering spell against the run of play. This streak of unpredictability made Shami irresistible, and it was instrumental in India winning more matches abroad, especially under Virat Kohli’s captaincy.Shami was also a great senior, who passed on his art and tricks of the trade to youngsters.“I learnt a lot of things from him during my time in the IPL. Subtle things like bowling at the death and with the semi-new ball,” Uttar Pradesh pacer Ankit Rajput said.At 36, Shami had been performing admirably in this Ranji season, picking up 14 wickets in his last three games. Yet, the constant snubs and time away from international cricket had hurt him.“He was trying hard to make a comeback. But after a point, he realised he was not going to get another chance in Tests, which is why he chose to retire,” Badruddin explained.“He wants to play the ODI World Cup next year. He has kept that window open,” he added. Shami is India’s highest wicket-taker in the 50-over World Cups, with 55 scalps from 18 games at an impressive average of 13.5.The sorcerer of seam signs off from Tests, leaving a gaping hole in India’s bowling roster. Finding Shami’s replacement would be as difficult as locating Sahaspur on the India map.
Article Summary: Mohammed Shami has announced his retirement from international cricket. The 36-year-old bowled with a big heart, indefatigable spirit, and unmatched skill over 64 Tests. He is India’s highest wicket-taker in the 50-over World Cups, with 55 scalps from 18 games at an impressive average of 13.5.
